hints: Notice all four options start with energy transferred but divide by a different quantity - charge, current, distance or time.
Recall the volt in base terms: $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J C}^{-1}$, so check which denominator gives joules per coulomb.
Compare $V = W/Q$ with $P = W/t$ to avoid confusing p.d. across a component with power dissipated in it.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: the definition of potential difference $V$ across a component in terms of energy transferred $W$.
State the governing relation: $V = W/Q$, where $Q$ is the charge moving through the component.
Check units: $W$ in joules $(\text{J})$ divided by $Q$ in coulombs $(\text{C})$ gives $\text{J C}^{-1}$, which is the volt $(\text{V})$.
Compare the other ratios: $W$ per unit time is power, and $W$ per unit distance is force, so they cannot be p.d.
Therefore energy transferred per unit charge matches $V = W/Q$. This is option A.

options.A: Correct - p.d. is $V = W/Q$, the electrical energy $W$ transferred per unit charge $Q$ passing through the component.
options.B: Incorrect - energy per unit current would divide by charge per unit time, which does not give $V = W/Q$ in volts.
options.C: Incorrect - energy per unit distance is force, not p.d., and ignores the charge moving through the component.
options.D: Incorrect - energy transferred per unit time is power $P = W/t$, not potential difference.
